title: What are the trade-offs between the Kafka compression codecs (`compression.type`) — `gzip` (highest ratio, highest CPU), `snappy` (fast, moderate ratio), `lz4` (very fast, low CPU), and `zstd` (strong ratio AND good speed, often the modern default) — why does producer-side batch compression reduce network and disk usage end-to-end, and why should producer and broker codecs be compatible?
shortTitle: What are the trade-offs between the Kafka compression codecs?

s1_definition.profdef: Kafka compresses a whole producer batch before transmitting it, controlled by `compression.type`. The codecs trade compression ratio against CPU cost. `gzip` gives the highest ratio but the highest CPU, `snappy` is fast with a moderate ratio, `lz4` is very fast with low CPU, and `zstd` offers a strong ratio and good speed, which is why it is often the modern default. Because the broker stores and forwards the compressed batch and only the consumer decompresses it, compression reduces network and disk usage end to end. Producer and broker codecs must be compatible so the broker can store the batch as produced without a costly recompress.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of National Bank of India mailing a stack of statements. Compression is like vacuum-packing the stack. `gzip` squeezes it the tightest but takes the longest at the packing machine. `snappy` and `lz4` pack quickly but less tightly. `zstd` is the modern machine that packs almost as tight as gzip but much faster. Because the vacuum-packed parcel stays sealed through the whole postal system and is only opened by the final recipient, it saves space on every truck and in every warehouse along the way, not just at the start.
s1_definition.oneliner: gzip squeezes hardest but burns CPU, lz4 and snappy are fast but looser, zstd is the balanced modern default, and compression pays off across network and disk because the batch stays compressed until the consumer opens it.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Kafka compresses a whole producer batch before transmitting it, controlled by `compression.type`. The codecs trade compression ratio against CPU cost. `gzip` gives the highest ratio but the highest CPU, `snappy` is fast with a moderate ratio, `lz4` is very fast with low CPU, and `zstd` offers a strong ratio and good speed, which is why it is often the modern default. Because the broker stores and forwards the compressed batch and only the consumer decompresses it, compression reduces network and disk usage end to end. Producer and broker codecs must be compatible so the broker can store the batch as produced without a costly recompress.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of National Bank of India mailing a stack of statements. Compression is like vacuum-packing the stack. `gzip` squeezes it the tightest but takes the longest at the packing machine. `snappy` and `lz4` pack quickly but less tightly. `zstd` is the modern machine that packs almost as tight as gzip but much faster. Because the vacuum-packed parcel stays sealed through the whole postal system and is only opened by the final recipient, it saves space on every truck and in every warehouse along the way, not just at the start.

**One line to remember:** gzip squeezes hardest but burns CPU, lz4 and snappy are fast but looser, zstd is the balanced modern default, and compression pays off across network and disk because the batch stays compressed until the consumer opens it.

sections.s2_technical:
The `compression.type` producer setting accepts `none`, `gzip`, `snappy`, `lz4`, or `zstd`. You set it with `props.put("compression.type", "zstd")`. The choice is a tradeoff between how small the batch becomes and how much CPU is spent compressing it.

`gzip` achieves the highest compression ratio, meaning the smallest output, but it uses the most CPU, so it is best when network or disk is the bottleneck and you have CPU to spare, or for cold data where ratio matters more than latency. `snappy`, built by Google, is fast with a moderate ratio and was a long-time default because it balances speed and size reasonably. `lz4` is very fast with low CPU and a ratio similar to or a bit better than snappy, so it is excellent for latency-sensitive high-throughput feeds. `zstd`, from Facebook, is the standout modern codec because it reaches close to gzip ratios while staying fast, and it has tunable levels, which is why many teams now default to `props.put("compression.type", "zstd")`.

Compression in Kafka is applied to the entire batch, not to each record, which is why a larger batch, encouraged by `linger.ms`, compresses better. Repetitive banking JSON with the same field names over and over compresses extremely well, often five to ten times smaller.

The end-to-end benefit comes from how Kafka handles the compressed batch. The producer compresses once. The broker, by default, stores the batch exactly as it received it, in compressed form, and forwards it to consumers still compressed. Only the consumer decompresses it to read the records. This means the savings apply on the producer-to-broker network hop, on the broker's disk, on replication between brokers, and on the broker-to-consumer network hop. One compression step pays off at every stage.

Producer and broker codec compatibility matters because of the broker setting `compression.type`, which defaults to `producer`, meaning keep whatever the producer sent. If you leave it as `producer`, the broker stores the batch as-is with zero extra CPU, which is ideal. If you force a different broker codec, the broker must decompress and recompress every batch, which costs significant CPU and defeats part of the benefit. So the recommended practice is to choose the codec on the producer and let the broker keep it. All modern brokers understand all these codecs, but a very old consumer might not understand a newer codec like zstd, so you must ensure your consumers support the codec you pick. A senior nuance is that for truly incompressible data, such as already-compressed images or encrypted blobs, compression wastes CPU for no gain, so you would use `none` there.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India streams transaction events to a central topic. The payloads are JSON with repeated field names, so they compress very well. The platform team must choose a codec that minimizes network and storage cost without starving the CPU during peak.

Problem 1 — without compression, the repetitive JSON floods the network and fills the brokers' disks quickly, forcing shorter retention. This is exactly what `compression.type` solves: the batch is squeezed before it travels and stays squeezed on disk.

Problem 2 — the team is unsure whether to pick the tightest codec or the fastest. This is exactly the gzip-versus-lz4-versus-zstd tradeoff: gzip saves the most space but may burn CPU under peak, while zstd gives almost the same savings with far less CPU.

Problem 3 — someone proposes forcing a broker-side codec different from the producer's. This is exactly the compatibility issue: that forces the broker to recompress every batch, wasting CPU, so the broker should keep the producer's codec.

The code will show a producer configured with each codec in turn, logging the configured codec and the relative payload size so the reader can reason about the tradeoff, and will note the broker keep-as-produced behaviour.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: ten thousand transaction events with repeated field names, roughly the same shape for Rajesh and Priya.

Step 1 — the producer accumulates events into a batch. Because linger is twenty milliseconds and the batch size is one hundred twenty-eight kilobytes, many events pack into one batch, which is ideal for compression.

Step 2 — with `none`, the batch travels and is stored at full size. With `gzip`, the batch is squeezed the most, so the fewest bytes travel and the least disk is used, but the producer spends the most CPU. With `snappy` or `lz4`, the batch is squeezed quickly but a bit less. With `zstd`, the batch is squeezed almost as tightly as gzip but much faster.

Step 3 — the batch arrives at the broker. Because the broker setting is keep-as-produced, the broker stores the compressed batch exactly as it received it, with zero extra CPU, and replicates the compressed form to followers.

Step 4 — the consumer fetches the still-compressed batch over the network, saving bandwidth on that hop too, and only then decompresses it to read the records.

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Producer: 10,000 repetitive TxnEvents → batch (128 KB, linger 20 ms)
    │
    ▼
  compress ONCE with compression.type
    ├─ gzip   : smallest bytes, highest CPU
    ├─ snappy : fast, moderate size
    ├─ lz4    : very fast, low CPU, moderate size
    └─ zstd   : near-gzip size, good speed  ← modern default
    │
    │ compressed batch travels the network (saves bandwidth hop 1)
    ▼
  Broker (compression.type=producer → KEEP as produced)
    │ store compressed on disk (saves disk)
    │ replicate compressed to ISR (saves inter-broker bandwidth)
    │
    │ forward compressed batch to consumer (saves bandwidth hop 2)
    ▼
  Consumer decompresses ONCE → reads records
    (one compress step pays off at every stage end-to-end)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Kafka compresses an entire producer batch before sending it, and the codec choice is a tradeoff between compression ratio and CPU cost. Gzip gives the highest ratio but the highest CPU, so it suits cold or archival data. Snappy is fast with a moderate ratio and was a long-time default. Lz4 is very fast with low CPU, which makes it great for latency-sensitive, high-throughput feeds. Zstd is the standout modern codec because it reaches close to gzip ratios while staying fast, which is why many teams now make it the default.

The reason compression pays off is that it is an end-to-end saving from a single compression step. The producer compresses once, the broker stores and replicates the batch still compressed, and it even forwards the compressed batch to consumers. Only the consumer decompresses it. So one compression step reduces bandwidth on the producer-to-broker hop, the disk on the broker, the bandwidth of replication between brokers, and the bandwidth to the consumer.

Producer and broker codec compatibility matters because the broker's compression setting defaults to keep-as-produced. If you leave it that way, the broker stores the batch exactly as the producer sent it with zero extra CPU. If you force a different broker codec, the broker has to decompress and recompress every batch, which wastes CPU and partly defeats the point. You also have to make sure your consumers understand the codec, because a very old client may not support a newer codec like zstd.

In my National Bank of India project, the transaction JSON was highly repetitive, so it compressed five to ten times smaller. We standardized on zstd on the producers because it gave us near-gzip space savings without the CPU hit under peak, and we left the brokers on keep-as-produced so they never recompressed. That cut our network and storage costs across the whole pipeline while keeping latency low.
